input: This explainer is concerned with the pump affinity laws, which are used to describe what happens to flow, head, and power when the speed of a centrifugal pump is changed. The central message is that the three quantities do not all respond in the same way. Flow is proportional to speed, head is proportional to speed squared, and power is proportional to speed cubed. In other words, each quantity has its own relationship with speed, and those relationships become progressively stronger as one moves from flow, through head, to power. Flow is the most straightforward case, because it simply follows speed in direct proportion. Head is somewhat less straightforward, because it depends on the square of the speed, which means that it responds more strongly than flow when the speed is altered. Power is the most sensitive of the three, because it depends on the cube of the speed, which means that it responds more strongly still. This point is illustrated by the worked check that is included in the passage. When the speed is doubled, the power is multiplied by 8. That result can seem surprising at first, but it follows directly from the cubic relationship between power and speed. More generally, the affinity laws provide a useful way of thinking about speed changes in centrifugal pumps, because they show that a single change in speed does not produce a single common change across all performance variables. Instead, flow, head, and power each follow the particular proportionality that applies to them, and the worked check on power is included to make the strength of the cubic relationship especially clear. The value 8 is the check's result, and it belongs to power rather than to flow or head.
target: Speed is the variable in this explainer, and the outcome is stated before the detail. For a centrifugal pump at varying speed, flow follows speed in direct proportion, head follows the square of speed, and power follows the cube of speed. The worked check is plain: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. Each law is read as a comparison between operating points of the pump at different speeds. The flow law is the simplest of the three. A proportional rise in speed gives the same proportional rise in flow, and a proportional fall in speed gives the same proportional fall in flow; the law is a statement of proportion, not a statement that flow is fixed by speed under every condition outside the comparison. The head law is stronger. Because head follows speed squared, the head comparison turns on the square of the speed change, so head moves by a larger proportion than flow for the same change in speed. The power law is stronger again. Because power follows speed cubed, the power comparison turns on the cube of the speed change. That cubic dependence is the point of the worked check. Doubling is a single change in speed, stated in words; applying the cube gives the stated power multiplier. The three laws should not be interchanged. Flow, head, and power are different quantities, and the affinity laws assign a different speed dependence to each: direct proportion for flow, the square for head, and the cube for power. A reader who applies the flow proportion to power understates the power change, and a reader who applies the power proportion to flow overstates the flow change. The explainer closes on the worked check because the check separates the laws in one case: doubling speed multiplies power by 8, while the flow and head changes are read from their own proportionalities, not from the power result.
